source.title: Sparse Autoencoders Learn Monosemantic Features in Vision-Language Models
source.authors: Mateusz Pach; Shyamgopal Karthik; Quentin Bouniot; S. Belongie; Zeynep Akata

record.tranche_reason: The study uses a different measure of neuron monosemanticity in vision-language encoders to examine whether sparse-autoencoder features are more interpretable than original neurons. It does not test the Qwen audit or language-model neuron explanations.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own neuron-level monosemanticity measurements, including comparisons with original vision-encoder neurons, which bear on V4. Its SAE steering results do not measure the share of interpretable neurons. Results cited from other work are not included.
record.test_reason: The study measures how monosemantic SAE latents are compared with raw neurons in vision encoders, and uses SAE latents to steer LLaVA. It does not test any version. It runs no Qwen or language-model neuron audit (V1, V2), no InceptionV1 cat-and-car analysis (V3), no attribution graphs (V5), and no held-out or simulation scoring of neuron explanations (V6, V7). The record links its rows to V4, but V4 concerns the share of interpretable native neurons, driven by tools and architecture. Here the improving 'tool' is an SAE that replaces neurons with learned latents; it does not explain more of the neurons themselves. The raw-neuron scores are all at the baseline floor (best = worst = 0.01 with DINOv2; about 0.48, roughly mean pairwise similarity, with CLIP ViT-B). That pattern means MS, which min-max normalizes over all 50k images, cannot separate a dense neuron with clean tails or poles from a polysemantic one. So the raw-neuron values cannot show whether native neurons have one main job. The findings are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that SAEs trained on VLMs substantially raise neuron-level monosemanticity relative to raw neurons, mainly through sparsity and wider latents, with Matryoshka SAEs best. They report that MS aligns with human judgments, and that SAE interventions on CLIP's vision encoder steer LLaVA, beating DiffMean on prompt adherence and content preservation.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies vision encoders with sparse autoencoders and an activation-weighted image-similarity score; it does not conduct the Qwen neuron-pole audit or test explanations on held-out activations.
record.method_sensitivity: MS varies with SAE expansion factor, sparsity K, layer, SAE variant, and the image encoder used to compute similarities.

fits_no_version.finding: In four vision encoders, final-layer raw neurons score MS 0.01 (at the floor), while Matryoshka SAE latents reach top MS of 0.59–0.92. In CLIP about 90% of same-width SAE latents score above the raw neurons.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE latents trained on vision-encoder activations are more monosemantic than raw neurons under an activation-weighted image-similarity score.

fits_no_version.finding: Stricter sparsity raises mean SAE latent MS (0.37 at K=1 to 0.07 at K=50) but lowers R2 (31.3% to 74.9%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In vision SAEs, monosemanticity of latents trades off against reconstruction quality.

fits_no_version.finding: Majority human choices agreed with MS in 82.8% of 1,000 neuron pairs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The MS score agrees with human judgments of image-set focus.

record.problems: The study is on vision encoders rather than language models. Its MS metric measures similarity among highly activating images, not whether each neuron has one human-nameable job; the cross-encoder table reports highest-scoring neurons rather than the fraction of all neurons meeting an interpretability criterion. The authors also note that high MS does not always produce precise steering effects.
record.rows_left_out: Not included: detailed layer-by-layer and expansion-factor MS tables for CLIP, further average/best/worst score tables, and additional plots in Sections 4.2 and Appendix E. These give further SAE and layer settings but do not change the main cross-encoder comparison or the reported same-width neuron fraction included here.

untested.parts: No language models, no scale sweep, no dense-versus-MoE comparison.
No InceptionV1 cat-and-car or pose analysis.
No share of interpretable native neurons under better explanation tools or across architectures. SAE latents replace neurons, and the raw-neuron MS sits at the metric floor.
No attribution graphs or replacement-model comparison.
No test of explanations predicting firing.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V4 'supports' and 'limits_scope' labels are removed. The SAE rows measure learned latents, not native neurons, and the raw-neuron MS is degenerate (identical floor value for all neurons, about 0.48 with a CLIP-B encoder, near the mean similarity). This degeneracy reflects min-max weighting over dense activations, so the study's 'raw neurons are polysemantic' picture is not evidence about whether neuron poles have one job. A reader might take the SAE results as tension with the essay's anti-superposition framing, but the study does not test that.

versions.untested_parts: No Qwen3-32B audit or estimates of one-job, two-job, or not-understood neuron poles.
The studied systems are vision encoders, not language models; no language-model scale sweep or dense-versus-MoE comparison.
No InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron, pose account, or recursive-generalization test.

The study compares SAE features with raw neurons and studies several vision encoders, but does not estimate an interpretable-neuron percentage comparable to the essay’s 5%–99% estimates, or isolate architecture and regularization as causes.
No attribution graphs or comparison with a trained replacement model.
No explanations assessed by predicting firing on held-out activating examples.
No automated scoring of neuron explanations by simulated activations on new text.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Matryoshka SAE comparisons with raw final-layer neurons in the four tested vision encoders
reader_labels.reason: Highest MS rises from 0.01 without an SAE to 0.59–0.83 at ×1 and 0.85–0.92 at ×4 across the tested encoders (r1–r12); about 90% of same-width SAE neurons score above original neurons in CLIP (r13).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Interpretability measured by MS, with sparsity varied in CLIP ViT-L
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports MS rather than a percentage of neurons judged to have one nameable job, and the mean score varies with sparsity; the strictest setting also has lower reconstruction quality (r14–r17).
